item.title: An Evolutionary-Economic Model of Reproduction and the Global Decline in Human Fertility — Thu Sep 3, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description: The global collapse in fertility rates poses a challenge to both economic and evolutionary models of human reproductive behavior. I develop a model of fertility, integrating evolutionary and economic approaches, that focuses on the costs and benefits of reproduction. The model derives offspring as positional goods, whose utility is entirely dependent upon their quality relative to the average quality of other offspring in the population. The model also derives adult quality as a positional good, its value dependent upon the average quality of other adults. Model predictions are for parental investment, offspring quality, and fertility are supported across a wide range of mammal species. As human populations transitioned from subsistence economies to industrialized economies, biological limits to offspring investment and adult quality were removed. item.title: Visualizing Cities and Historic Spaces: 15 Years of Research in Art History and Digital Visual Studies — Fri Sep 4, 9:00 AM — Smith Warehouse
item.description: For over a decade, the Art, Art History & Visual Studies Department at Duke has conducted research on using digital methods to explore the visual and historical problems associated with the cultural history of cities. Such work, in conjunction with colleagues at both workshops at the University of Venice as well as the University of Padua, has resulted in a productive international collaboration on modeling, mapping, and critically analyzing historical building sites, objects in space, and cultural experience. This scholarly core has in turn expanded to include cultural geographers, literary scholars, historians, engineers, and digital visualization specialists who, together, have created a vibrant community meant to intervene in the critical analysis of art objects and/in urban sites. This conference extends this work by highlighting the critical use of digital methods to analyze historical cities and related spatial cultural environments in Digital Humanities and Visual Culture today

item.title: Social influences on eating across the lifespan — Fri Sep 4, 11:00 AM — None
item.description:
As humans eat a variety of foods (compared to generalist species that eat a limited variety of foods), every day we make choices regarding what and how much to eat. In addition to our individual taste preferences and goals, we also are influenced by other people in our food choices. In this talk, I will discuss existing theoretical frameworks and research from my lab that examines social influences on eating behavior. Specifically, I will discuss research on (1) children's beliefs about foods from diverse cultural backgrounds, (2) observational and experimental studies of social modeling in infancy, and (3) an ongoing intervention providing peer counseling to Latine mothers as they navigate breastfeeding.

item.title: Flipping the Bird Friday — Fri Sep 4, 12:15 PM — Rubenstein Library Mary Duke Biddle Room
item.description:
Duke University Libraries will be turning the pages of the Birds of America on the first Friday of every month! We welcome you to stop by and watch-what bird will be next?
Birds of America is one of the greatest undertakings in the history of both art and ornithology. Almost 200 years after its publication, it remains a primary resource for scientists and scholars. This four-volume, double-elephant-folio edition on handmade paper measures three feet tall and two feet wide and comprises 435 hand-colored prints impressed from copperplate engravings. Of the original 175 to 200 complete sets, 125 have survived. Nine species of those depicted have since gone extinct.
Source: Duke University

Jaylen Coleman is a former Duke football player and biomedical engineer with a Master's degree in engineering management, building technology at the intersection of sports, movement, and performance. item.description:

The series kicks off on Saturday, September 5, with Zootopia 2 (PG)! The 2025 animated film will delight audiences of all ages with the story of Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde, two new partners in the Zootopia Police Department with clashing personalities. The film stars Ginnifer Goodwin as Judy Hopps and Jason Bateman as Nick Wilde. All movies will be shown at Durham Central Park, located at 501 Foster Street, from 7:30-9:30 p.m. DPR will be offering free popcorn and there will be an amazing selection of local food trucks during each event. item.title: Turning headlines into humor with Bryan Tucker — Mon Sep 14, 6:00 PM — Carroll Hall
item.description:
UNC Hussman School of Journalism and Media alumnus Bryan Tucker ’93 has written for Saturday Night Live for 20 years. During his time at SNL, he’s had to find humor through four different presidents, an economic crisis, a pandemic and two Duke basketball championships. It wasn’t always easy.
In this seminar, Tucker takes students through some of the news events of the past two decades and gives insight on how SNL approached those events as comedy fodder for millions of viewers. Tucker will show clips and provide a firsthand look at the decisions and process of turning news into sketches.
This event is hosted by the UNC Hussman School of Journalism and Media and is open to the public. Learn more.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.description:
“Access, Activism, and Aesthetic Revision: Crip Methods for Art History”
This talk brings together the core arguments of The Agency of Access: Contemporary Disability Art and Institutional Critique (2024), Hospital Aesthetics: Disability, Medicine, Activism (2025), and Rehabilitating the Asylum: Mental Health Justice and Contemporary Art (2027) to demonstrate that disability is not peripheral to canonical art; instead, it is one of its most generative methodological engines to arise with the canon of 20th century art history. Across these three books, Amanda Cachia develops what she calls a critical-aesthetic approach to access, care, and confinement, tracing how hospitals, asylums, and contemporary art institutions function as overlapping architectures of power, creativity, and resistance. item.description:
The UNC Center for Media Law and Policy will celebrate First Amendment Day on Wednesday, October 7, 2026.
This campuswide, daylong series of events is designed to both celebrate the First Amendment and explore its role in the lives of Carolina students. Students and other members of the University community will read from banned books and discuss the public university’s special role as a marketplace of ideas and the need to be tolerant when others exercise their rights. As always, First Amendment Day is observed during National Banned Books Week.
First Amendment Day is free and open to the public. For a full schedule of First Amendment Day events, please visit FirstAmendmentDay.unc.edu.
UNC students can register for CLE credit on Heel Life.

item.description:
Triangle Developers Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.
**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.
Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.
See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.
